text: Christopher Ndarathi Mūrūngarū, born on August 19, 1954, in Nyeri, Kenya, is a former Kenyan politician who served as a Member of Parliament for Kieni Constituency in Nyeri District and as a former Minister of Transport. When the National Rainbow Coalition (NARC) Government took power from the Kenya African National Union (KANU) in 2003, Dr Mūrūngarū was appointed Minister for Internal Security; he was later transferred to the Ministry of Transport following revelations of the Anglo-Leasing scandal, which he did not expressly deny. After President Mwai Kibaki reconstituted the cabinet following a defeat in the November 21, 2005 Kenyan constitutional referendum, Mūrūngarū was removed from the cabinet. He was a close ally of President Mwai Kibaki. Mūrūngarū has been in conflict with the British Government over the cancellation of his visa to enter the United Kingdom due to allegations of corruption in the Anglo-Leasing scandal, and he has taken the British Government to court to challenge the cancellation. He has hired prominent Kenyan lawyer Paul Muite and British lawyers, including Mr Rabinder Singh, a Queen's Counsel of Matrix Chambers, London, Mr Richard Stein, a senior partner in Leigh, Day and Company, and Ms Tessa Hetherington, a junior counsel of Matrix, to represent him. On November 23, 2005, President Mwai Kibaki dissolved his cabinet after losing the constitutional referendum, prompting a cabinet reconstitution. On January 22, 2006, John Githongo named Mūrūngarū as one of three top politicians—along with Kiraitu Murungi, former Justice Minister and current Energy Minister, and Finance Minister David Mwiraria—involved in a financial scam involving up to US$600 million. On February 1, 2006, Finance Minister David Mwiraria announced his resignation to allow for investigation, a move welcomed by many Kenyans though seen by some as a scapegoat to protect a president whose support was waning. On January 16, 2006, President Kibaki permitted anti-corruption chief Aaron Ringera to request Mūrūngarū to declare and account for his wealth; Mūrūngarū has since moved to court to block the Kenya Anti-Corruption Commission (KACC) investigation, claiming it would amount to self-incrimination. On February 2, 2006, Vice President Moody Awori announced he would not resign despite being implicated in the Anglo-Leasing scandal, insisting on his innocence and stating that only due process would compel his resignation; he has faced criticism for defending those involved in the scandal before Parliament. On February 17, 2006, the KACC arraigned Mūrūngarū in Nairobi court for failing to declare and account for his wealth, citing rapid accumulation of wealth linked to the Anglo-Leasing scandal; Mūrūngarū denied refusing to declare his wealth and was released on a bond of KSh200,000. On December 1, 2006, the Kenyan High Court ruled that KACC's notice to Mūrūngarū was not conducted in accordance with the law, quashing the case, though it did not halt KACC's investigation into corruption, emphasizing that any orders must follow legal procedures. A society known as the Name and Shame Corruption Network (NASCON) held a demonstration in Nairobi to demand the resignation of senior figures in President Mwai Kibaki's administration, including civil service boss Francis Muthaura and Vice President Moody Awori. In May 2022, the Court of Appeal in Kenya reduced the fine payable to Mūrūngarū by Githongo from KSh27 million (US$228,000) to KSh10 million (US$84,000) after Mūrūngarū successfully sued Githongo for leaking a dossier implicating him in the Anglo-Leasing scandal. In what was seen as an upset, Mūrūngarū was defeated by a less prominent candidate in the Party of National Unity's primary elections for parliamentary candidates in November 2007.
